strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear identification of HLS development bottlenecks and practical relevance
VODA (Verification-Oriented Data Augmentation) is a pragmatic paradigm for dynamically capturing and expanding error case datasets
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with 612 test cases across 33 HLS designs and 34 error types, including comparisons with multiple LLM baselines and existing methods
Thorough ablation studies demonstrating the contribution of individual components (fine-tuning, analysis agent, DPO, iterative refinement)
Strong empirical results: 82.7% pass rate on error repair (17% improvement over GPT-4o), 3.6× geometric mean speedup on optimization tasks
Clear system architecture and well-designed multi-agent framework with specialized agents for distinct phases (generation, debugging, optimization)
Effective presentation with informative figures and workflow diagrams
weaknesses: CRITICAL: Fundamental scope mismatch with ACL—this is a hardware design automation paper, not a computational linguistics or NLP contribution. The work does not address core language understanding, linguistic modeling, or NLP methodologies, and would be far more appropriate for DAC, ICCAD, or hardware design conferences

Limited novelty in LLM/NLP methodology: uses standard LoRA fine-tuning, applies existing DPO technique without domain adaptation, and employs straightforward error-type-based agent routing with no linguistic or LLM architectural innovation

Data construction quality concerns: Insufficient validation that LLM-injected bugs are realistic; unclear breakdown of how many error types were discovered vs. manually enumerated; no demonstration that synthetic bugs trigger similar failure modes as real errors

Limited experimental scope: Only 5 linear algebra kernels (PolyBench) used for optimization evaluation, providing minimal algorithmic diversity; evaluation tied to proprietary Xilinx ZCU106 hardware with no evidence of generalization to other platforms or HLS tools

Reproducibility issues: Relies on proprietary Xilinx Vitis HLS tool (expensive, non-open-source); no mention of code/dataset release; missing critical implementation details (exact prompts, HLS output parsing, RAG mechanism, latency measurements)

Evaluation methodology limitations: Unfair comparison with general LLMs (expected that fine-tuned models outperform)—lacks nuance; incomplete baselines (HeteroRefactor, HeteroGen mentioned but not compared); ad-hoc energy efficiency proxy metric (Eq. 2) with unjustified functional forms; no user studies or practical utility validation

Insufficient failure analysis: 17.3% failure rate not analyzed; no breakdown of error types that remain unsolved or design patterns that break the system; limited discussion of out-of-distribution behavior

Generalization claims inadequately supported: Only 5 test kernels limit statistical significance of generalization claims; no analysis of how performance scales to diverse problem types or larger designs

Training details underspecified: No ablation on hyperparameter choices (why 11 epochs SFT + 3 epochs RL?); preference dataset construction for DPO (3,489 pairs) not well documented; no multi-run statistics or confidence intervals reported

System cost analysis missing: No latency measurements for full optimization+debugging cycle; up to 5 iterations required in some cases with no analysis of iteration distribution; no practical computational budget validation

strengths: Addresses a practical and important problem in hardware design automation
Comprehensive end-to-end system integrating both error correction and design optimization
Strong empirical results on 612 error cases with 82.7% repair pass rate and 3.6× average speedup
Extensive evaluation across multiple baselines including general LLMs, DSL-based, and learning-based methods
weaknesses: Critical scope mismatch: This is a hardware design automation paper, not an NLP/computational linguistics contribution; completely inappropriate for ACL 2026
Limited technical novelty: Multi-agent LLMs, SFT, DPO, and RAG are standard techniques; VODA is basic error injection, not a sophisticated augmentation paradigm
Severe experimental limitations: Only 5 PolyBench kernels (all linear algebra); no evaluation on diverse application domains or real industry hardware designs; test-training overlap unclear
Over-engineered system design: 10 different LLM agents with unclear responsibilities and no analysis of computational cost; simpler alternatives not explored

Reproducibility severely compromised: Heavy proprietary tool dependence (Vitis HLS, Xilinx), no code/dataset release, vague implementation details, sparse training documentation, BugRAG insufficiently specified
Weak statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing; single-run results; ablation study only shows aggregate results

Questionable design choices: Energy efficiency metric (Eq. 2) appears ad-hoc without justification; comparisons against Vitis auto mode (not learning-based) make contribution assessment difficult; 14.8× speedup claim needs deeper validation
Incomplete analysis: No failure case analysis, no computational cost analysis, DPO yields only 1.8% improvement yet adds complexity, no analysis of iterative refinement latency

Overstated claims: VODA presented as 'pioneering' when it is standard error injection; 'verification-oriented' is just verifying errors occur; semantic alignment among agents asserted but not explained

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine bottlenecks in HLS development with clear articulation of existing approach limitations
Novel VODA paradigm that systematically constructs HLS-specific error datasets through verification-oriented bug injection, capturing 34 error types across hierarchically organized BugRAG
Strong empirical results: 82.7% repair pass rate (19.1% above GPT-4o, 63% above Llama3-8B) on 612 diverse test cases, with comprehensive ablation studies validating each component
Comprehensive system design addressing both error correction and optimization end-to-end, integrating hierarchical reasoning in HLSFixer and iterative refinement in HLSTuner

Thorough experimental evaluation across multiple dimensions (Kernel/Vitis/Manual test sets, multiple baseline comparisons, performance vs. DSL-based methods) with careful separation of train/test distributions
Clear presentation with effective workflow diagrams (Figures 3-5) and systematic documentation of error categories with debugging instructions
weaknesses: Questionable relevance for ACL 2026: This is primarily a hardware design automation paper that applies LLMs as a tool, not a computational linguistics or NLP contribution. It does not advance understanding of language processing, language models, or core NLP techniques

Limited technical novelty in LLM methodology: Relies on standard LoRA fine-tuning, existing DPO approach, and conventional multi-agent patterns; novelty is primarily in domain application rather than LLM technique development

Narrow evaluation scope limiting generalization claims: HLSTuner evaluated on only 5 kernels (acknowledged as minimally sufficient), restricted to linear algebra workloads, single HLS tool (Vitis 2022.1) and platform (Xilinx ZCU106); generalization to other tools/platforms unexplored

Critical reproducibility concerns: No commitment to release code/data, exact prompts not provided, 'golden results' generation procedure vague, training requires 8 A800-80G GPUs, implementation details incomplete

Dataset quality and representativeness issues: 307 manually crafted designs may introduce bias, bug injection process may not capture real-world error distributions, no cross-validation or dataset quality validation procedures, no discussion of potential distributional shift

Lack of statistical rigor: No confidence intervals, significance testing, or cross-validation despite small sample sizes (5 kernels); Energy Efficiency metric (Eq. 2) uses arbitrary exponential decay formulation lacking justification; multi-LLM evaluation strategy computationally expensive with no cost-benefit analysis
Incomplete failure analysis: 17.3% of error repairs fail with no characterization of failure modes, patterns, or cases where HLSFixer breaks down; limited discussion of generalization boundaries

Missing and incomplete comparisons: HLSPilot (cited but not compared), no simple few-shot prompting baselines with larger models, comparison with DSL-based methods somewhat apples-to-oranges (fundamentally different paradigms)

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing real HLS design bottlenecks (data scarcity, design space exploration, debugging complexity)
Comprehensive system design with principled multi-component architecture and clear separation of concerns
Strong empirical results: 93.4% debugging pass@1 vs 60.6% for Gemini-3-pro; 18.1× speedup over baseline; post-implementation validation confirms feasibility
Thoughtful dataset construction including VODA's self-evolving error mechanism and 33-category BugRAG, with proper train-test separation analysis
Thorough experimental validation with ablation studies, multiple benchmarks (108 generation tasks, 591 debugging cases), and comprehensive baseline comparisons
Detailed reproducibility documentation covering training settings, prompt design, and experimental protocols
weaknesses: Critical scope mismatch: This is hardware design automation research, not computational linguistics. It lacks novel NLP/CL methodology and would be better suited for DAC, ICCAD, or ASPLOS venues rather than ACL

Significant practical limitations severely restrict applicability: only supports loop-level directives (PIPELINE, UNROLL, ARRAY_PARTITION), excludes critical DATAFLOW and AXI interfaces, validated on single hardware platform (Xilinx ZCU106)
Heavy dependence on specialized fine-tuning of Qwen-2.5-Coder-14B; unclear how much improvement derives from system design vs. fine-tuning; generalization to other LLM families unexplored
Circular reasoning in VODA: using LLM-generated errors to train LLMs to fix LLM-generated errors; unclear transfer to human-written buggy code; no evaluation on real human bugs

Insufficient experimental rigor: no statistical significance testing or error bars on pass rates; limited baseline scope; unfair comparisons to general-purpose LLMs not designed for HLS; small optimization dataset (4,804 samples from 20 kernels) raises overfitting concerns
Reproducibility limitations: fine-tuned models and code not provided; dependency on proprietary Xilinx Vitis HLS 2022.1; no public dataset release mentioned
Unclear generalization: no evaluation on HLS patterns outside training distribution, mixed loop+dataflow designs, or larger complex designs; no failure mode analysis

CoT generation bias and circular logic: teacher model introduces implicit biases; RAG baseline in Section E.1 may reflect suboptimal chunking rather than RAG limitations; alternative CoT strategies not explored

strengths: Comprehensive end-to-end system addressing HLS generation, debugging, and optimization
Extensive experimental evaluation with detailed ablation studies and supplementary analyses
Well-motivated problem statement with clear articulation of HLS design challenges
Structured error categorization in VODA with 33 modular error types
Detailed implementation information and reproducibility attempts in appendices
weaknesses: Fundamental scope mismatch: This is an EDA/hardware design paper, not an NLP paper suitable for ACL
No novel LLM methodology: Relies entirely on standard SFT, DPO, and prompting techniques from prior work
Unfair experimental comparisons: Compares specialized fine-tuned models against general-purpose LLMs not designed for HLS
Questionable data augmentation validity: Error injection strategy may not transfer to real HLS bugs; no validation provided

Overcomplicated architecture: Uses 10+ LLMs (LLM①-LLM⑩) with unclear differentiation and no ablation justifying this complexity

strengths: Comprehensive multi-agent LLM framework addressing real and well-motivated HLS design bottlenecks
Strong experimental results with 32.6% debugging improvement, 41.8% generation success improvement, and 18.1× speedup vs. baseline
Rigorous methodology including ablation studies (16.6% from analysis agent, 3.7% from DPO), train-test similarity analysis (Rouge-L < 0.15), and post-implementation validation
Thorough dataset construction with 10,878 buggy code samples across 33 HLS-specific error types organized in structured BugRAG
Practical system with reasonable runtime (<30 min optimization) that preserves functional semantics and integrates with vendor tools
Extensive documentation with detailed implementation details, prompts, training hyperparameters, and appendices supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Fundamental venue misalignment: This is a hardware design automation system using LLMs, not computational linguistics research; minimal novel NLP methodology (standard fine-tuning, RAG, DPO, CoT)
Severely limited generalization scope: Single FPGA platform (Xilinx ZCU106), single HLS tool (Vitis), limited to specific directives (no DATAFLOW/AXI), and primarily synthetic benchmarks

Data quality concerns: All training data generated by DeepSeek-V3.2 (potential contamination), BugRAG constructed from ad-hoc sources, synthetic error injection may not reflect real-world scenarios, and Appendix G.1 shows DeepSeek memorization on PolyBench

Limited technical novelty: HLSFixer uses straightforward prompt engineering, HLSTuner applies NSGA-II + standard LLM reasoning, VODA is incremental error case expansion; contribution is domain integration rather than algorithmic innovation

Evaluation limitations: pass@k only measures success not optimization quality, speedups from synthesis simulation not post-implementation timing, no statistical significance testing, modest improvements on complex accelerators (2.3×/1.3×), and only 16 workloads in post-implementation validation

Unfair baseline comparisons: General-purpose LLMs not designed for HLS, different access methods, different temperature settings (0.7 vs. 0.1), RAG baselines receive only documentation while ChatHLS uses structured training data—contributions not properly isolated

Reproducibility gaps: Fine-tuned models not released, sparse dataset composition/provenance details, unjustified training choices (why 2 DPO epochs? why rank 8 LoRA?), critical prompt engineering without sensitivity analysis

Methodological concerns: pass@20 may not reflect practical deployment costs, only 15 optimization iterations tested, no sensitivity analysis for 80% resource constraint, multi-agent overhead substantial (Figures 15-17) with unclear accuracy-efficiency trade-offs
